raw_case_text:
An eight-year-old girl presented with painful blisters on the skin of 40 days duration. She also had fever with chills, cough, dyspnoea, and severe headache for the past one month. She had suffered from chickenpox four months back, which resolved uneventfully. She was anemic, and had stunted growth. Chest examination revealed bilateral crepitations. She also had neck stiffness.
Multiple painful and tender vesicles and bullae of varying size were seen all over the body, predominantly over the acral areas. Few bullae were hemorrhagic. Warty excrescences were seen overlying some blisters. Oral erosions were noted. The skin lesions started as tiny vesicles [Figure 1], which evolved into larger bullae, some of them were hemorrhagic [Figure 2]. Thereafter, they progressed to form warty excrescences [Figure 3], and finally resolved with varioliform scars. New lesions continued to appear, even as the older ones healed. Oral erosions were also present. There was no dermatomal grouping of the skin lesions.
Due to the unusual morphology of the lesions, enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV was done, which turned out to be positive. Western blot for HIV was also positive. Her parents were HIV negative. There was no history suggestive of sexual abuse. No possible explanation could be offered for the HIV positivity of the child, other than frequent, and possibly unsafe intramuscular injections in the past.
Tzanck smear from the blisters showed multinucleated giant cells [Figure 4]. Histopathology of the early vesicle revealed typical features of varicella blister, and that of late warty lesions showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis without the classical features of viral blister.
Chest x-ray showed pneumonitis, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytosis. Complete hemogram was normal except for dimorphic anemia. Her CD4 count was 41, blood VDRL was nonreactive, and serum IgG and IgM for HSV-1 and HSV-2 were negative. Serum IgM for VZV was negative, but IgG for VZV was positive in very high titre.
The patient was started on antiretroviral therapy comprising three drugs: stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine. Intravenous acyclovir in the dose of 10 mg/kg body weight was administered for three weeks. There was dramatic improvement with complete resolution of the skin lesions, meningitis, and pneumonitis. At the end of third week, acyclovir was stopped and the patient was discharged. However, the blisters promptly recurred within two weeks. This time oral acyclovir was started with the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, and the lesions subsided again. At present, the child is on antiretroviral therapy and oral acyclovir with the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, for the past three months. Her general condition is improving, but the occasional vesicle still continues to appear. It has been planned to continue acyclovir with the same dose till her CD4 count improves substantially.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old girl presented with a 40-day history of painful generalized skin blisters and a 1-month history of fever with chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having recovered uneventfully from primary varicella (chickenpox) 4 months earlier, the child developedcrops of painful vesicles and hemorrhagic bullae 40 days prior to presentation that evolved into hyperkeratotic warty excrescences and varioliform scars while new blisters continued to erupt. For the 1 month preceding admission, she also experienced fever with chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.
subjective.past_medical_history: Primary chickenpox 4 months prior; history of stunted growth and frequent, potentially unsafe intramuscular injections in the past. Both parents tested HIV-negative, and there was no history of sexual abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful/hemorrhagic skin blisters, oral erosions, fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, and severe headache.

objective.physical_examination: Anemic and growth-stunted child with nuchal rigidity and bilateral pulmonary crepitations on auscultation. Mucocutaneous examination revealed oral mucosal erosions and generalized non-dermatomal painful vesicles, hemorrhagic bullae, overlying verrucous/warty excrescences, and varioliform scars predominantly distributed over the acral extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete hemogram showed dimorphic anemia with normal leukocyte and platelet counts. Blood VDRL and serum HSV-1 and HSV-2 IgG/IgM were negative; serum VZV IgM was negative while serum VZV IgG was strongly positive in very high titer. Tzanck smear of blister fluid demonstrated multinucleated giant cells. Chest X-ray showed bilateral pneumonitis.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 41 cells/µL. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis consistent with viral meningitis. Skin biopsy histopathology of an early vesicle showed classic intraepidermal varicella viral blistering, whereas biopsy of a late verrucous lesion demonstrated hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated chronic verrucous/bullous varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection complicated by VZV pneumonitis and aseptic lymphocytic meningitis unmasking horizontally acquired pediatric AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, confirmatory HIV Western blot, CD4+ count 41 cells/µL, high-titer VZV IgG, and multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear). The child was initiated on triple antiretroviral therapy (stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine) plus intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) for 3 weeks, achieving complete resolution of skin lesions, pneumonitis, and meningitis. When cutaneous vesicles recurred 2 weeks after stopping IV acyclovir, long-term suppressive oral acyclovir (80 mg/kg/day in four divided doses) was instituted alongside ART, maintaining clinical control at 3-month follow-up pending substantial CD4+ recovery.
